draft.title: The Vietnam War and conscription
card: During the Cold War, Australia and its ally the United States feared that communism would spread through Asia. Australia joined the war in Vietnam to try to stop that spread.
Australia sent military advisers to South Vietnam from 1962. They trained South Vietnamese soldiers. From 1965 Australia sent combat troops.
Conscription means the government requires people to serve in the military. Australia called up 20-year-old men by a ballot, a lottery based on birth dates.
Men whose birthdays were drawn had to serve if they were called up. Conscripts served alongside volunteers in the army.
draft.remember: Australia fought in Vietnam to stop communism spreading, and conscripts were chosen by a birthday ballot.

a.q: Why did Australia send troops to the war in Vietnam?
opts: To try to stop communism spreading through Asia
To defend Australia from an invasion by Vietnam
To win new land for Australia in South-East Asia
To help the United States end its own civil war
a.why: Australia and the United States feared communism would spread through Asia, and Australia joined the war to try to stop it. Vietnam was not threatening to invade Australia, so defence from invasion is not the reason.
a.clue: Think about what Cold War governments feared.

b.q: In 1966, Tom turns 20 in Adelaide. His birthday is drawn in the ballot and he is called up. What has happened to Tom?
opts: He has been conscripted and must serve in the army
He has been given the choice to volunteer or to refuse
He has been sent to Vietnam only as a military adviser
He has been placed in a reserve and cannot be sent overseas
b.why: Conscription means the government requires people to serve, and the birthday ballot chose who was called up. Tom had no choice to refuse, so volunteering is wrong. The card does not say conscripts were limited to advising or to home service.

a.best: To try to stop communism spreading through Asia

b.best: He has been conscripted and must serve in the army

problems.detail: The why says 'Tom had no choice to refuse'. That overstates it: balloted men could apply for conscientious objector status, and some draft resisters refused to serve and faced penalties. 'Was legally required to serve' would be accurate.

The card never says that conscripts were sent to fight in Vietnam (from 1966), although the point says the combat troops included conscripts. It only says conscripts served alongside volunteers in the army. So ruling out 'cannot be sent overseas' in question b relies on outside knowledge.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The why for b overstates that conscripts could not refuse, since conscientious objection existed. The card also does not say that conscripts were sent to Vietnam, which is central to the point.

He must legally serve but cannot be sent to Vietnam
He may choose freely whether to serve or stay home
He may go to Vietnam but only as a military adviser
